slides.title: Questions That Actually Explore
bullets: Open-ended questions designed to uncover real clinical experience and reasoning
Not designed to confirm something the MSL already believes
Not answerable with a simple yes or no
The single most important tool for turning a visit into a genuine conversation

slides.title: Start With What, How or Why
bullets: "Do you" and "is it" invite a closed, low-information answer
"What," "how" and "why" require the other person to explain their thinking
Example: a broad open question invites a substantive response instead of one word

slides.title: Specific, Not Narrow or Leading
bullets: Too broad — "how do you approach this disease" — fails to generate focused insight
Too narrow and leading — implying an answer — is a disguised statement, not a question
A well-scoped question is useful without presupposing the answer

slides.title: Sequence From Broad to Specific
bullets: Start broad to set the surrounding clinical context
Narrow toward the specific scientific question the MSL needs answered
Jumping straight to a narrow question often produces a thinner answer

slides.title: Stay Open to Uncomfortable Answers
bullets: Exploratory questions must stay open to answers unfavourable to the product
Only asking when a favourable answer is expected is not really exploring
Pivoting to informing whenever a conversation gets uncomfortable undermines credibility

takeaway.title: Exploratory questions turn a scientific visit from information delivery into real insight generation
bullets: What, how and why questions open genuine dialogue; do you and is it close it down
Good questions are specific without presupposing the answer
Genuine exploring means staying open even to unfavourable answers
